articles.title: Hiring bias against transgender women depends on both identity and appearance, field experiment suggests
articles.summary: In a field experiment involving more than 10,000 job applications in Germany, trans women who disclosed their identity or had male-coded facial features each received about 10 percent fewer positive responses from employers. When both signals were present, the penalty jumped to 32 percent.

articles.title: Many people judge candidates and policies by a single deciding feature, new research suggests
articles.summary: Many survey methods assume people weigh every feature of a candidate or policy. New research suggests most don’t: mental shortcuts dominated, and the strategy people used often shifted from one issue to the next.

articles.title: Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger
articles.summary: Yale scientists have uncovered how the stress hormone cortisol helps the brain turn emotional experiences into stronger, longer-lasting memories. The discovery reveals that stress can reshape communication between brain networks involved in emotion and memory, potentially explaining why certain moments are so difficult to forget.

articles.title: Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
articles.summary: For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.

articles.title: Oxytocin amplifies negative childhood memories for anxiously attached adults
articles.summary: Oxytocin is often called the "love hormone," but new research shows it can actually amplify negative childhood memories for people who experience relationship anxiety. The hormone appears to heighten our sensitivity to social cues, rather than simply boosting affection.

articles.title: Some adults’ brains look older than their age, and gut biology may be part of the picture
articles.summary: Some adults’ brains look “older” than their age long before old age. In a study of 1,400+ people aged 18 to 65, older-looking brain patterns were linked to somewhat weaker working memory, more depressive symptoms, and subtle gut differences.

articles.title: Family genetics study questions the role of genetic nurture in ADHD
articles.summary: A large study of families suggests that a child's own DNA drives their ADHD traits by mid-childhood, finding no robust evidence that parents' genetics indirectly shape these behaviors through the household environment.

articles.title: Your job says little about what you want in a partner, study suggests
articles.summary: Does a nurse want a different kind of partner than an engineer? In a study of nearly 2,000 adults across seven countries, the industry people worked in had almost no link to what they prioritized in a partner.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
articles.summary: Even under general anesthesia, the human brain can analyze language, recognize different types of words, and predict what comes next in a story, according to a surprising discovery by Baylor researchers. The findings challenge our understanding of consciousness and suggest that the unconscious brain is far more capable than scientists previously realized.

articles.title: Strokes have nearly doubled among younger adults, and scientists aren't sure why
articles.summary: Strokes are becoming alarmingly common among younger adults, with rates nearly doubling among people ages 20 to 54 over nearly three decades. Researchers found that blocked blood vessels in the brain accounted for much of the increase, while high blood pressure, diabetes, and substance use also became more common among younger stroke patients. Although survival rates have improved, more young adults may now face the lasting consequences of stroke.

articles.title: Rare study reveals a striking divide inside an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain
articles.summary: A rare examination of an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain revealed that regions cleared of amyloid plaques had remarkably little of the harmful tau buildup associated with memory loss, while neighboring areas showed extensive damage. The discovery suggests that removing amyloid may have lasting protective effects and could help slow Alzheimer’s progression, especially when treatment begins early.

articles.summary: arXiv:2610.20665v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time. We introduce RealtimeBench, with 180 tasks across six game types, to evaluate agents while games continue running during inference. articles.summary: arXiv:2610.20667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rapid advances in AI capabilities are causing benchmarks to saturate. Yet benchmark items produce far more information than the scores we typically extract from them: a full transcript of how each model solved the task. articles.title: AlphaDiana: A Measurement System for Agents in Verifiable Reasoning Tasks
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.20675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents pair reasoning models with harnesses that organize model calls, execute tools, load skill instructions, and retain history in memory. Understanding agent performance requires linking execution conditions to outcomes, behavior, and resource use. We introduce AlphaDiana, a measurement system with modular interfaces for datasets, agents, environments, and scorers. It preserves harness-native control loops while controlling file reuse and memory retention separately. AlphaDiana supports macro analyses of complete agents and micro interventions
